title: Retrospective data analysis with prospective telephone follow-up on the use of MonoMax® suture material in the third and fourth layers of the Shouldice hernia repair
summary:
The Shouldice technique is an established standard procedure for the surgical repair of inguinal hernias (groin hernias). It involves stitching together the patient's own tissue layers to reinforce the weakened abdominal wall. International clinical guidelines recommend this technique as one option for the surgical treatment of inguinal hernias.

Traditionally, non-absorbable sutures are used in the Shouldice procedure. These sutures remain permanently in the body and are intended to ensure long-term stability of the repaired tissue. However, permanently implanted suture material may be associated with complications for some  patients, including chronic pain, foreign-body reactions, and other long-term problems.

Modern, slowly absorbable suture materials may offer an alternative. They are designed to provide sufficient stability during the healing process and gradually break down in the body over time. This could reduce the amount of foreign material remaining permanently in the body without compromising the long-term stability of the surgical repair.

The aim of this study is to investigate the safety and effectiveness of a modified Shouldice procedure using a so-called hybrid technique. The Shouldice repair consists of four rows of sutures. In the two deeper rows (rows 1 and 2), non-absorbable suture material continues to be used. In the two more superficial rows (rows 3 and 4), a slowly absorbable suture material (MonoMax®) is used instead. This approach aims to maintain the stability of the surgical repair while reducing the amount of suture material that remains permanently in the body.

The main objective of the study is to determine whether this hybrid technique provides a safe and durable repair of inguinal hernias. Particular attention will be paid to the recurrence of inguinal hernias and to patient-reported outcomes, including symptoms and quality of life during long-term follow-up.

For the study, eligible patients will first be identified using existing medical records. They will then receive written information about the study and be invited to participate voluntarily. After providing informed consent, participants will undergo a standardized telephone interview. This interview will collect information on hernia recurrence, possible symptoms, and other health-related outcomes.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Primary inguinal hernia repair using the Shouldice technique with Hybrid approach (MonoMax® in suture rows 3 and 4).
Exclusion criteria:
Recurrent hernias
Prior surgeries in the inguinal region
MonoMax® wasn't used
Lack of informed consent
Inability to provide informed consent
